analogy.p: Think of a photograph on your phone. Zooming in (magnification) makes the picture bigger, but whether you can tell two nearby objects apart depends on how many pixels the camera captured (resolution). If you zoom in on a low-quality picture, the image gets bigger but just becomes a blurry mess. An electron microscope is like a camera with an enormous number of pixels: you can zoom in far and still see crisp detail. The analogy breaks down because on a phone resolution is fixed by the sensor, but in a microscope resolution depends on the wavelength of the radiation used, and electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.

bullets: Know the **two types of microscope** and the key differences: magnification and **resolving power** (resolution).

Explain how **electron microscopy** let biologists see **sub-cellular structures** (mitochondria, ribosomes, plasmids, the detail of the nucleus) in much finer detail than the light microscope allowed.
Use the equation **magnification = image size ÷ real size** and rearrange it for any of the three quantities.
Convert between **mm, µm and nm** and express very small or large numbers in **standard form** (Higher tier skill that is tested on this point).
Carry out **Required Practical 1**: prepare a slide, focus the microscope, draw a labelled biological drawing and calculate magnification.
Link to other topics: cell structure (4.1.1.1-2), cell differentiation, stem cells and, in later topics, bacteria and pathogens (which can only be seen with the microscope).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8461 section 4.1.1 expects you to compare **light microscopes** and **electron microscopes**, to explain how electron microscopy has increased our understanding of **sub-cellular structures**, and to carry out calculations involving **magnification, real size and image size**. Required practical 1 is the hands-on part: you must use a light microscope to observe, draw and label a selection of plant and animal cells, and include a magnification calculation. Exam questions on this point are almost always worth marks you can secure with careful method and unit handling.

bullets: **Magnification** = how much larger the image appears compared with the real object (written ×100, ×400 etc.).
**Resolving power / resolution** = the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as two separate points.
Good resolution gives a **sharp, detailed image**; poor resolution gives a blurred image where close structures merge into one.

The resolution is limited by the **wavelength of the radiation used** to form the image: light has a relatively long wavelength, while electron beams have a much shorter one, so electron microscopes resolve far finer detail.
Examiner trap: do not say an electron microscope is 'stronger' or 'zooms in more' and stop there; always state **both higher magnification AND higher resolving power**.
Because the useful magnification is set by the resolution, there is **no point increasing magnification beyond what the resolution allows**.
core.h: Why we need microscopes: magnification and resolution
core.p: Most cells are far too small to see with the naked eye, and the structures inside them are smaller still. A microscope solves this in two different ways, and the exam tests that you know they are not the same thing. **Magnification** is how many times bigger the image is than the real object. **Resolution** (resolving power) is the ability to distinguish between two points that are very close together as two separate points. A microscope can make an image bigger without making it any clearer; if the resolution is poor, extra magnification only produces a bigger blur.

bullets: **Eyepiece lens** (usually ×10): you look through it; magnifies the image formed by the objective lens.
**Objective lenses** (commonly ×4, ×10, ×40) on a **revolving nosepiece**: you rotate to choose the magnification. Total magnification = eyepiece × objective, e.g. ×10 × ×40 = **×400**.
**Stage**: the flat platform that supports the slide; **stage clips** hold the slide in place.
**Light source (lamp or mirror)** and sometimes a **diaphragm**: provides and controls the light passing up through the specimen. The specimen must be thin so light can pass through it.
**Coarse focus knob**: moves the stage (or tube) a large distance to bring the specimen roughly into focus. **Fine focus knob**: small movements for a sharp image.
**Arm** and **base**: the frame; carry the microscope with one hand on the arm and one under the base.
Light microscopes are cheap, portable and can view **living cells**, but have limited magnification (up to about ×1500) and resolution.
core.h: The light microscope: parts and what each does
core.p: The light microscope shines light through a thin, transparent specimen and uses glass lenses to form an enlarged image. The total magnification is found by multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece lens by the magnification of the objective lens being used. Learning the parts and their jobs is a regular 2-3 mark question.

bullets: **Much higher magnification** (can be over a million times) and **much higher resolving power** than a light microscope.
Allows us to study cells in **much finer detail** and see **sub-cellular structures** such as the internal structure of **mitochondria and chloroplasts**, **ribosomes**, and **plasmids**.

Disadvantages (useful for evaluation questions): the instrument is **large, very expensive and needs training**; specimens must be prepared in a **vacuum**, so **living specimens cannot be viewed**; the image is black and white (colour may be added by computer).

Beyond the spec but helpful: the **transmission electron microscope (TEM)** sends electrons through a very thin slice, giving 2D internal detail; the **scanning electron microscope (SEM)** bounces electrons off the surface, giving 3D surface images.
Because of electron microscopy, scientists could link **structure to function** in organelles, e.g. the folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion (cristae) gives a large surface area for respiration.
Link to other topics: knowledge of ribosomes as the site of protein synthesis and mitochondria as the site of aerobic respiration depends on this kind of imaging.
core.p: An electron microscope uses a beam of **electrons** instead of light, focused by electromagnets instead of glass lenses. Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than visible light, so the microscope has a much greater **resolving power** and can be used at a much higher **magnification**. This is what allowed biologists to see the fine detail of sub-cellular structures for the first time.

bullets: **Radiation used**: light microscope uses visible light; electron microscope uses a beam of electrons.
**Magnification**: light up to about ×1500; electron far higher (over ×1 000 000).
**Resolving power**: light about 200 nm (0.2 µm); electron roughly 0.2 nm, about a thousand times better, so electron microscopes show much finer detail.
**Living specimens**: light microscope can view living cells; electron microscope cannot (vacuum, preparation kills the cells).
**Cost and size**: light microscope cheap and portable; electron microscope very expensive, large, needs trained operators.
**Image**: light microscope gives a coloured image (especially when stained); electron microscope gives a black and white image.

**What is visible**: light microscope shows nucleus, cytoplasm, cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole; electron microscope also shows ribosomes, internal membranes of mitochondria, plasmids and fine detail of the nucleus.
core.h: Light microscope versus electron microscope: comparison
core.p: A comparison question might ask you to give two differences, or to evaluate which microscope to use. Use a clear point-by-point structure and always compare the same feature for both microscopes (never leave the comparison half-finished).

bullets: Structures such as **ribosomes** are too small to be resolved by a light microscope; electron microscopes showed them, leading to understanding of **protein synthesis**.
The inner structure of **mitochondria** (folded cristae) could be seen, linking the structure to its role in **aerobic respiration** by increasing surface area for enzymes.
**Plasmids** and the arrangement of DNA in prokaryotic cells could be studied in more detail.
The structure of the **cell membrane** and the **nucleus** (nuclear pores, chromatin) could be examined more closely.

Model phrase for 2 marks: 'Electron microscopes have a higher magnification and higher resolving power, so they show more detail of sub-cellular structures, which helps scientists understand how structures are related to their functions.'
This shows the idea that **advances in technology lead to advances in scientific understanding**; new evidence can change or extend previous models.
core.p: Before electron microscopes, biologists could see the cell membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm but could not make out the smaller organelles. When electron microscopes became available, the much greater resolving power revealed the detailed structure of organelles, which led directly to understanding what they do. This is the kind of 'how has technology helped science' idea the specification asks for.

bullets: **magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object**
Rearranged: **size of image = magnification × size of real object** and **size of real object = size of image ÷ magnification**.
Magnification has **no units** (it is a ratio), but the image and real size must be in the **same units** before dividing.
In the formula triangle put **I** on top and **M** and **A** (actual) underneath; cover the one you want.
The image size is usually measured with a **ruler in mm** on a drawing or photograph; the real size is often in µm.
If a question gives the total magnification of a microscope (e.g. ×400) and the field of view or drawing size, you can find the real size of a cell by **dividing the image size by 400**.
Always check your answer is sensible: a typical plant cell is about **100 µm** (0.1 mm) long; a bacterium a few µm; a mitochondrion around 1-2 µm.
core.p: The key equation for this point is magnification = image size ÷ real size. This is the equation you must be able to rearrange. It is on your list of equations you need to remember for GCSE biology (it is not given on the paper), so learn it with the triangle method: I over M × A.

bullets: **1 mm = 1000 µm** (micrometres); **1 µm = 1000 nm** (nanometres); so **1 mm = 1 000 000 nm**.
To go from a bigger unit to a smaller unit **multiply**; to go from a smaller unit to a bigger unit **divide**.
**Standard form**: a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10. Example: 0.0045 mm = **4.5 × 10⁻³ mm**; 45 000 nm = **4.5 × 10⁴ nm**.
Convert **before** you divide: change the image size and real size into the same unit first (usually µm).
Prefix meanings from the spec: **centi** (1/100), **milli** (1/1000), **micro** (1/1 000 000), **nano** (1/1 000 000 000).
Check: a bigger unit means a smaller number; 45 µm is a smaller number than 45 000 nm because the unit is bigger.
core.h: Units and standard form (Higher tier skill)
core.p: Mistakes with units are the most common reason students lose marks on magnification questions. Know the conversions and be prepared to give answers in standard form, which is a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

bullets: Step 1: **Write the formula** you need (M = I ÷ A, or A = I ÷ M, or I = M × A).
Step 2: **Measure or read** the image size (ruler in mm) and note the real size or magnification.
Step 3: **Convert so both lengths are in the same unit** (e.g. mm to µm by × 1000).
Step 4: **Substitute and calculate**. Show every line.
Step 5: **State the answer** with the correct unit (no unit for magnification, µm or mm for a length) and check it is sensible.
Scale bars: measure the scale bar with a ruler, then **magnification = measured length of scale bar ÷ real length it represents** (same units). Then use this magnification to find other sizes.
Worked example: image of a mitochondrion measures 30 mm and the magnification is ×15 000, so real size = 30 ÷ 15 000 = **0.002 mm = 2 µm**.
core.p: Use the same approach every time so that you gain method marks even if the arithmetic goes wrong. Write the equation, substitute with units, convert units, then calculate, and finally give the answer with the correct unit or in standard form if asked.

bullets: **Method (onion epidermis):** place a **drop of water** (or iodine solution) in the middle of a clean slide.
Use **forceps** to peel a very thin layer of epidermis from the inside of an onion layer; lay it **flat** on the drop. It must be **one cell thick** so light can pass through it.
Add a **drop of iodine solution** (a stain). **Stain** makes structures such as the nucleus and cell wall show up more clearly because different parts absorb the stain differently.
Lower a **coverslip** onto the slide at an angle using a **mounted needle**, then lower it slowly. This **avoids trapping air bubbles**, which would obscure the view.
Clip the slide on the stage. Select the **lowest power objective lens** first. Use the **coarse focus** to move the lens close, then the **fine focus** for a sharp image.
Move up to a **higher power objective** and refocus **using the fine focus only** so that the lens does not hit and break the slide.
**Safety:** handle glass slides and coverslips carefully; iodine can stain skin and clothes; wash hands; do not point a mirror microscope at the sun.
Link: the same method with **methylene blue** stains animal (cheek) cells; the nucleus and cytoplasm show up but there is no cell wall, chloroplast or large vacuole.
core.h: Required Practical 1: preparing a slide and using a light microscope
core.p: In this practical you prepare a temporary slide of plant cells (usually a thin layer of onion epidermis) and view it with a light microscope, then draw and label what you see and calculate the magnification. Animal cells can be viewed using cheek cells scraped from the inside of the mouth and stained with methylene blue. You must be able to describe the method in the correct order.

bullets: Use **clear, continuous lines**, no sketching; draw only what you can see, not what you think should be there.
The drawing should be **large** (fill at least half the space) and drawn in **proportion**.
Draw **label lines with a ruler**, not crossing each other, and ending exactly at the structure being labelled; write labels **horizontally** and outside the drawing.
Give the drawing a **title** and state the **magnification** used (for example, 'Onion epidermal cells ×400').
Draw a few cells carefully rather than the whole field of view; show the **cell wall as a double line** for plant cells.

Typical visible structures: **plant cell** - cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole (chloroplasts if from a leaf, not onion epidermis); **animal cell** - cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus.
core.h: Drawing and labelling cells: biological drawing rules
core.p: Marks are awarded for the quality of a biological drawing. The examiner wants a clear, accurate scientific drawing, not an artistic sketch. Use a **sharp pencil** and a clean eraser; **no colouring or shading**.

bullets: **Image blurred or too dark**: the specimen is too thick (light cannot pass through) - use a **thinner layer**; or the **focus** is wrong - refocus using fine focus; or adjust the light/diaphragm.
**Cells not visible / unclear nucleus**: no stain, or stain not left long enough - add iodine or methylene blue.
**Measuring the image**: using a ruler to measure a drawing has an error of ±0.5 mm; measuring **several cells and finding a mean** improves accuracy.
**Drawing errors**: drawings are subjective - use a photograph or scale bar to improve accuracy.
**Calibration**: a graticule (eyepiece scale) calibrated against a stage micrometer gives measurements in µm without needing to calculate (beyond GCSE but a useful idea).
**Sampling**: the cell you drew may not be typical; look at several areas of the slide.
core.h: Evaluating the practical and sources of error
core.p: Higher tier questions often ask why a result or image was poor, or how the method could be improved. You need to link the problem to its cause and fix. **Air bubbles** under the coverslip: caused by dropping the coverslip flat; lower it slowly at an angle with a needle.

bullets: **Surface area to volume** and **diffusion** questions may give cell images and ask for real sizes.

**Required practicals** later in the course (osmosis, enzymes) do not use the microscope, but **plant tissue**, **stomata** and **cell division (mitosis)** practicals do use microscopes and magnification.
**Microorganisms**: pathogens like bacteria and protists can only be seen using microscopes; understanding of disease is built on this.
**Graph/photograph skills**: given a photomicrograph with a scale bar, you are expected to calculate magnification and then the size of a labelled structure.
**Extended writing**: for a 6 mark 'compare microscopes' question, give at least 3 detailed comparisons with both microscopes mentioned and a conclusion about which is better for a given purpose.
core.h: Exam links and harder ideas to connect
core.p: Magnification questions turn up in many other topics, so being fluent here earns marks across the whole of paper 1. Examiners also like to combine magnification with biological reasoning. **Cell size comparisons**: bacteria (about 1-10 µm), animal cells (about 10-30 µm), plant cells (about 100 µm); organelles are smaller still. Use these to check if answers are sensible.

exam: **State / Name (1 mark)**: e.g. 'State what is meant by resolution' - 'the ability to distinguish between two points close together' (a point-by-point definition earns the mark).
**Compare (2-3 marks)**: always mention BOTH microscopes. 'Electron microscopes have higher resolving power than light microscopes' is a full mark; 'higher' on its own is not.

**Explain how electron microscopy increased understanding (2-3 marks)**: higher magnification + higher resolving power → sub-cellular structures (give an example such as ribosomes/mitochondria) seen in more detail → understanding of their functions.
**Calculation (2-3 marks)**: 1 mark equation / substitution, 1 mark unit conversion, 1 mark correct answer with unit. Show working because a wrong answer with correct method still gets 2 of 3.
**Measure with a ruler** on the printed diagram: measure to the nearest mm; examiners allow a tolerance (e.g. ±1 mm) but check your unit.
**Standard form (1 mark)**: if the question says 'give your answer in standard form', unrounded decimals will not get the mark.

**Describe the practical (4 marks)**: use ordered steps - thin tissue, drop of stain, coverslip at an angle, low power first, coarse then fine focus. Mention **why** (thin so light passes through, angle to avoid bubbles).
**Biological drawing (usually 3-4 marks)**: size, continuous lines, accurate proportions, labels with ruled lines, title/magnification.
**Evaluate (6 marks)**: structure into advantages of each microscope, a link to a specific context (e.g. viewing living cells vs viewing ribosomes), and a justified conclusion.
**Scale bar questions**: measure the bar in mm, convert to the unit of the label, divide to get magnification, then use it for other structures.
**Command words**: 'calculate' = a number; 'explain' = give a reason using 'because'; 'suggest' = apply your knowledge to an unfamiliar context.

mistakes.r: Higher magnification AND higher resolving power, so more detail is seen.
mistakes.w: An electron microscope has a higher magnification only.

mistakes.r: Magnification is how much bigger the image is; resolution is how clearly two close points are distinguished.
mistakes.w: Magnification and resolution are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Include the unit (0.1125 mm) and convert if asked (112.5 µm).
mistakes.w: Dividing 45 mm by 400 and giving the answer as 0.1125 with no unit.

mistakes.r: Convert both to the same unit first (e.g. mm to µm × 1000).
mistakes.w: Using image size and real size in different units in the formula.

mistakes.r: Divide by 1000 to go from µm to mm (smaller unit to bigger unit = divide).
mistakes.w: Multiplying by 1000 to go from µm to mm.

mistakes.r: Standard form needs a number between 1 and 10: 4.5 × 10⁻³.
Specimens are in a vacuum and are killed, so living cells cannot be viewed.
mistakes.w: Electron microscopes can look at living cells.

mistakes.r: Always start with the lowest power objective lens and use coarse then fine focus.
mistakes.w: Using high power first when focusing.

mistakes.r: Lower it at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles.
mistakes.w: Adding the coverslip flat so it drops quickly.

mistakes.r: Use sharp pencil lines only, with ruled label lines and a title with the magnification.

summary: AQA expects you to compare light and electron microscopes (magnification and resolving power), explain how electron microscopy revealed sub-cellular structures, and calculate magnification, image size and real size using correct units and standard form. Required Practical 1 (preparing a slide and using a light microscope) is tested in both method and calculation form. These are reliable marks if your units and method are careful.

terms.d: How many times larger the image of an object appears compared with the real object; magnification = image size ÷ real size.
The ability to distinguish between two points close together as separate points; the higher the resolving power, the more detail seen.
A microscope that uses visible light and glass lenses to produce an enlarged image; can view living cells.
A microscope that uses a beam of electrons; has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope.
Structures found inside cells, such as the nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts and plasmids.
The lens you look through in a light microscope, usually ×10.
The lens closest to the specimen; several of different magnifications on the revolving nosepiece.
Eyepiece lens magnification multiplied by objective lens magnification.
Knob that moves the stage or lens large distances to bring the specimen roughly into focus.
Knob that makes small adjustments to give a sharp image.
A dye (for example iodine or methylene blue) that makes parts of cells show up more clearly.
A thin piece of glass or plastic placed over the specimen to flatten it and protect the lens.
A unit of length equal to one thousandth of a millimetre (1 × 10⁻⁶ m).
A unit of length equal to one thousandth of a micrometre (1 × 10⁻⁹ m).
A number written as a × 10ⁿ where a is between 1 and 10 and n is a whole number.
A line on a micrograph that represents a known real length, used to calculate magnification.
The sample of biological material being observed under the microscope.

worked.q: A student draws a cell seen with a light microscope. The drawing is 52 mm long. The total magnification is ×800. Calculate the real length of the cell in µm. (3 marks)
steps: Equation: real size = image size ÷ magnification.
Check: a plant cell around 100 µm is typical, so 65 µm is sensible.

worked.q: A micrograph of a plant cell has a scale bar 25 mm long labelled '50 µm'. The cell on the image measures 40 mm. Calculate the magnification and the real width of the cell. (4 marks)
steps: Convert the scale bar to µm: 25 mm = 25 × 1000 = 25 000 µm.
Real width of cell = 40 mm ÷ 500 = 0.08 mm.

worked.ans: Place a drop of water on a clean slide. Peel a thin layer of epidermis from the onion with forceps and lay it flat on the drop. Add a drop of iodine to stain the cells. Lower a coverslip at an angle using a mounted needle to avoid trapping air bubbles. Place the slide on the stage, select the lowest power objective lens and use the coarse focus knob then the fine focus knob to get a clear image. Change to a higher power objective and refocus with the fine focus only.
worked.q: Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion cells and use a light microscope to view them. (4 marks)
steps: Plan: thin tissue, stain, coverslip, then low to high power focusing.
